OOP, Lecture 1Introduction to object-oriented programming

A class is the mold. An object is what comes out of it.

Say "dog" and everyone pictures something with four legs that barks. That shared idea is a class: abstract, nobody can pet it. Rex the Dalmatian asleep on your sofa is an object: real, specific, with his own name and age. Build a few.


        

        

        
Dashed outline means class (a definition). Solid yellow means object (a real thing in memory).

      

      

        

        

      

    


    
Two terms the lecture separates

    
Object orientation is a way of thinking about and designing a solution: look at a problem and see the "things" in it. Object-oriented programming is the coding style that follows from it: a program built from objects, where each object holds data (called fields or attributes) and code (called methods). Not every language supports this. C, for example, doesn't have classes.


    
What you just did, in the lecture's words

    
    
      
  • Everything is an object. Dogs, cars, hotel rooms, bank accounts.
    • 
      
  • Every object has a type, its class. The type of dog1 is Dog.
    • 
      
  • The class defines characteristics and operations. Dog lists name, breed, age, and the operations bark() and birthday().
    • 
      
  • Every object holds its own exact values. Rex is a Dalmatian, Bella is a Yorkshire Terrier. Same class, different values.
    • 
      
  • A program is objects telling each other what to do by sending messages. Each method button sends a message, like dog1.bark().
    • 
      
  • Each object has its own memory, and can be made of other objects. Call birthday() on one dog and only that dog gets older. A Car could contain an Engine object.
    •

Classes stack from general to specific

    
The lecture's Vehicle diagram. Each level down adds detail, and everything a parent has, its children get automatically. Tap a class.

    

    

      

      

    

    
Reading up the tree is generalization: Sedan and Hatchback share enough that you invent "Car" for what they have in common. Reading down is specialization: start broad, add detail. The slide writes "from generalization to specification"; it means specialization.

    
Analogy: job titles. "Employee" is general. "Engineer" is an Employee plus technical skills. "AI Engineer" is an Engineer plus ML. Each title carries everything above it. And you never meet "an Employee" in the abstract; you meet Sara, who happens to be one. Sara is the object.

    

  


  
  

    
How programming got to objects

    
Five stages, each fixing the previous one's biggest pain. To make the differences visible, every stage solves the same job: keep track of two bank accounts.

    

    

    

  


  
  

    
Abstract data types: the direct ancestor of classes

    
An ADT is a new type you design yourself: a set of values plus the operations allowed on them, defined by what they do, not by how they're coded.

    

    
Analogy: a vending machine. You know its operations: insert coin, choose item, get change. You know nothing about its wiring, and you don't need to. Any machine offering those same operations is "the same type" to you, whatever is inside.


    
1. Abstraction: keep only what the purpose needs

    
Abstraction means reducing a real thing to the information relevant for a particular purpose. A real person has thousands of details. Which ones belong in your system? Strike out what doesn't matter, then check. Then switch the purpose and try again: the same person gives a different model.

    

    

      

        

        

        

      

      

        
2. The model you're building

        

        
A model is the abstract view of the problem: the data that matters plus the operations on it. An ADT is a kind of model.

      

    


    
3. The three properties of an ADT

    
    
      
  1. It's a well-defined entity you can handle as one unit: "a BankClient", not loose variables floating around.
    2. 
      
  2. It defines the data structure of its items: name, date of birth, ID, account number.
    3. 
      
  3. That data can only be accessed through defined operations: createAccount, deposit, withdraw. No reaching in.
    4. 
    

    
Anything with all three is an abstract data type.


    
4. Encapsulation: data and operations sealed in one capsule

    
Encapsulation bundles the data and its operations together and keeps the details away from whoever uses the ADT. Try breaking each account.

    

      

        
Open box

        

        
acc.balance =

        
balance: 1000

        

      

      

        
Capsule

        

        
acc.balance =

        
acc.withdraw()

        
acc.deposit()

        
balance: 1000

        

      

    

    
Analogy: an ATM. You never open the vault. You ask the machine to withdraw, and it checks the rules first. The vault is the private data; the ATM buttons are the public methods.

    
Why bother

    

      
ModularityThe Account can be built, tested and fixed on its own.

      
Controlled accessEvery change goes through a method that can say no.

      
Interface vs implementationRewrite the inside freely; code using withdraw() never notices.

      
Extends built-in typesOnce defined, Account a; works like int x;.

The four pillars

    
The lecture's ring diagram has six pieces: class and object are the building blocks; encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism are the four principles built on them.

    


    
Encapsulation vs abstraction

    
These two get confused in every exam. Both hide things, but different things for different reasons.

    

      
AbstractionEncapsulation

      
        
HidesIrrelevant detailsInternal data and how operations work

        
LevelDesign levelImplementation level

        
QuestionWhat matters for this problem?How do I protect the inside?

        
ExampleBankClient has no hair colorprivate balance, changed only by withdraw()

        
Car analogyTo a driver, a car is a wheel, pedals and a gear stickThe engine sits under a closed hood; you press the pedal, you don't inject fuel yourself

      
    

    
The lecture defines data abstraction as finding a class (the general type) from the real objects that represent it, which is what you did with the dogs and the vehicle tree.

    Overriding. A subclass replaces a method it inherited. Every variable below has the same declared type, Animal, yet each call runs a different version, chosen at runtime by the actual object. Untick a box to remove that override.
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    

    
    Heads-up on the slide's wording
    Slide 29 says overloading's meaning is "implied by the code itself" (read: by the different parameter lists you wrote) and overriding's is "implied by the values of the supplied variables" (read: by which object the variable actually points to at runtime, not the numbers inside it). Compile time vs runtime is the cleanest way to remember the difference.
    

    
    Inheritance: build on what exists
    
    
    A new class takes the attributes and methods of an existing one and adds its own, with extends in Java. That's the Vehicle tree: class Car extends WheeledVehicle. You don't rewrite move() for every vehicle.

    Object-oriented languages
    
    
    The languages from the lecture, in order. The pill shows the date the slide gives where it differs from the commonly cited release.
    
    
    
    
      
    
      Others mentioned: Eiffel (the slide spells it "Effile"), Objective-C (Apple's main language before Swift), and Ada (object orientation added in Ada 95).
      
    
      About those dates
      Languages have a "work started" date and a "first released" date, so sources disagree by a year or two. If an exam asks, use the slide's numbers; that's what your professor will mark against.
      

    
      Is Python a pure OO language?
      
    
      "Pure" means everything is an object and all data is reached only through methods. Smalltalk is the classic pure one. Python is OO, and in Python even numbers and functions are objects, but it doesn't enforce privacy: a leading underscore is only a polite "please don't touch".
      
    
      
    
      Java isn't pure either, for the opposite reason: private is enforced, but primitives like int and double are not objects.
